events.title: Kink is Political: Accountability
events.description:
In our last session before a short summer break, we’ll turn towards the concept of “accountability.”  In conversation with Pinko’s published volume After Accountability: A Critical Genealogy of a Concept, we’ll trace the history and limitations of a value commonly professed by kink educators and organizations. We’ll work to understand the terms widespread popularization and adoption, theoretical context, and use within policy and incident response policies within kink and sex positive spaces. We’ll ask: what does it mean to be held accountable? Who is empowered and disempowered by the concept of accountability? Who does the concept disenfranchise, and what model of human psychology and experience do popular versions of the concept of accountability propose?  
About this series
Kink is Political is an online discussion with Addie Tahl, Georg Barkas, Andrea Rimon, and occasional special guests. Participants are invited to join a discussion during which we unite critique with an emphasis on the practical and day-to-day issues and challenges of kink, intimacy, and relationships. 
Focusing on concepts central to BDSM, leather, rope, and sex-positive communities, it interrogates widely adopted approaches and commonly held notions. It aims to understand the politics of kink beyond the language of sexual liberation and politics of sexual liberalism, both frames that have proven insufficient in addressing widespread harm, a rising international tide of sex-negativity and reaction, or in guaranteeing that the most marginalized can sexually flourish. 
Kink is Political is an examination of the contexts and consequences of how we talk about and understand gender and sexuality. It is a forum to think about how kink spaces and practices operate, what works, what doesn’t, and what we can use to build something better.

events.title: Desire Mapping – Understanding and Communicating Your Wants
events.description:
Desire mapping is a guided exploration of your desires, boundaries, and how to express them confidently with others. Led by Ceci, a skilled sex therapist, this session offers a safe space to navigate common questions and challenges around sexuality, desires, and communication. 
Through reflective exercises, group discussion, and shared insights, you’ll learn how to tune into your desires, identify your boundaries, and express them authentically. Whether you’re looking to deepen your self-awareness, improve communication in intimate relationships, or work through confusion around sexual wants, this workshop is a powerful starting point. 
This workshop is inclusive, trauma-informed, and open to individuals of all genders, orientations, and relationship structures within LGBTQIA+ identities. You will be asked to work in small groups and pairs with other participants. 
What to expect from this workshop

Understand and embrace your desires
Define your boundaries and learn how to recognize when they come up spontaneously
Learn to communicate desires and boundaries both in theory and practice

Who should attend

Anyone curious about their own desires or feeling disconnected from them
People seeking to improve communication in intimate or sexual relationships
Those navigating consent, boundaries, or changes in desire or sexual identity

Please note that this is an LGBTQIA+ only event. Any identities and experience levels within this umbrella are very welcome and affirmed.

Seth Sjöström (*2000) is a bass player and composer from northern Sweden currently based Berlin. With a foundation in Jazz, free improvisation and Swedish folk music, he's constantly looking for new ways to express himself as well as communicating with others through art. He's greatly inspired by the harsh but honest nature of northern Sweden and is driven by the will to use music as a tool to build a genuine connection to himself, other people and the world around him.

Deeply personal yet widely resonant, his songwriting has connected with audiences and musicians worldwide, with his work recorded by artists from Emilia Mårtensson to the RTV Slovenian Big Band. In his own words, his music is rooted in a belief that songs can help people better understand themselves and their lives.

events.title: Karada House Queer Summer Party
events.description:
Our “new” space is already turning three (!!) so we’re having a queer little summer party about it. 
Come hang out, dance, play games, eat daddy Antje’s sausages, lie in a cuddle puddle, make new friends, avoid eye contact with the new friends, and generally exist together in a nice way. It’s a sober space, but still very much a party. 
This is for LGBTQIA+ folks – extroverts, introverts, socially anxious cuties, people who say “I’ll only stay for one hour” and then don’t leave. You can be in the middle of everything or tucked away somewhere cozy. Both are correct. 
There’s no pressure to do anything in particular — just drift between things and see what feels good. 
We’ll also have a clothing swap, so bring stuff you don’t wear anymore and maybe leave as a slightly different person. There will be a crafts and games room, so bring your summer crochets and art projects to work on in company. 
Spaces:

kitchen + mezzanine: snacks, alcohol-free drinks for sale, soft socializing
main room: dancing, social games, performances, a cuddle area (!!)
corner room: crafty queers + board games + gentle, quiet(er) vibes
garden (if weather behaves): BBQ, clothing swap & freebox, lying on the grass
(if not, we simply bring “outside energy” inside)

Program
14.00 Doors open 
14.30 Social Games & Facilitated Dance Party with Ceci Ferox
Awkward is today’s word, and we will embrace it. Waddle like a penguin, or let the spirit of our house octopus plushie guide your moves. The weirder, the better. Also maybe learn (and forget) some people’s names? We don’t know, but this is for all the introverts who don’t know how to people (and the extroverts who want to adopt us… eh, them). 
15.30 Trans* Choir Plänterwald (TCP’22)
“We are Berlin’s powerful choir, featuring original arrangements for trans*, non-binary, and inter* voices. With a blend of fun retro hits and contemporary pop songs, we create a space for openness, visibility, and community. Our repertoire is as diverse as we are: at times loud and defiant, at others gentle and moving—but always authentic. Our goal: a safe space to discover one’s own voice and grow together.” 
16-18 Hanging out & Pop-up performances: 

Community Tarot Reading with Caritia
Caritia is a Berlin-based kink activist, shibari educator, and co-founder of Karada House and OhYesPlease.org. Caritia’s art stems from a desire to advocate and support others to explore intentionally and intersectionally the boundaries around their bodies, sexuality and self-expression.
Surprise Performance with Quentin Crisper and Peppi The Brutalist Panda
Urban nature scout, radical faerie, playmate and adhd-prince, based in Berlin Quentin Crisper explores the world
through bodywork, sex work and art. Quentin aims to be a constant invitation for people to explore the strange, the intimate, the magical and the longings and desires in the unspoken spaces in between.  — Daydreaming, awkward, and hot. Peppi is a Berlin-based performer and activist with an acute passion for seriously silly kink. Their interests include voice work, chaos and non-normative powerplay. A complete menace, they often live by the motto “that’s stupid… I’ll do it!”.

18-21 Karaoke with Ceci Ferox
Come find your voice in a traditional Finnish karaoke, where your choice of song matters more than how you sing it. Sit in a corner with the microphone, avoiding eye contact with the audience, or ask a cutie to dance while someone sings a tango.

drop in whenever, but get a ticket beforehand
not a play space

events.title: BIPOC Utopias: Ace & Aro
events.description:
This month, we will offer space to discuss what it is to be Ace and/or Aro, as a BIPOC individual. Covering what these words/terms mean and diving into how we can support ourselves and others from a play context. 
This is a monthly separatist space to discuss and lab about kink, intimacy, and virtual play space for black, brown and Indigenous folks. 
For quite some time, Caritia has been musing on how to encourage and inspire more BIPOC into the realm of alternative lifestyles and ways of relating. There are many systemic barriers to this, including patriarchy, capitalism, classism and racism. In an effort to change the narrative, Caritia wishes to offer a monthly gathering for BIPOC to talk, learn about a topic or practice, and support one another through a community actively built together, with the aspiration to gather in person once a year. 
Caritia’s intention is to create a guided, active space for learning and coming together. This format has the potential to morph and change as the group sees fit.

Winchester’s industrial soundscaping suggests mainframes on the fritz and nuclear cores in meltdown, dystopian sci-fi fantasies playing out on a galactic scale.”
Pitchfork
Adam Winchester is an electronic musician and live performer whose work applies dub mixing techniques to experimental electronic music. His live sets centre on the mixer as an instrument, using delay, echo, and spatial processing to reshape bass driven rhythms, found sounds, modular synthesis, bespoke instruments, feedback systems, and heavily manipulated samples in real time.
With roots in Bristol’s dubstep scene as Wedge, and a long-running practice operating between bass music and exploratory sound design, Winchester has developed a distinctive approach that prioritises space, repetition, and gradual transformation fused with tropes of Dub, IDM and the hardcore continuum. He has released on revered labels Osiris Music, Soil, and Mindwaves, with a forthcoming LP on Oval Harmonique set to drop on vinyl later this year.
Alongside solo work, his collaborative projects include Wrecked Lightship and Dot Product, with acclaimed releases on Midnight Shift, and Peak Oil, spanning experimental performance, club contexts, and installation work. His music also involves collaborations with Renate Knaup of Amon Düül II, the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, and Japanese Noise artist KK Nüll, alongside performances at festivals including Berlin Atonal, Krake, and Boiler Room.

events.title: Intro to Suspension
events.description:
The goal of suspension, in Addie’s understanding, is not to do the most difficult thing or last the longest or take the most impressive picture, but to enjoy an adventure, support a partnership, stay focused on humans rather than patterns, and tailor the experience to best suit the individuals involved.

This two-part class is suitable for people who have never suspended but have a general idea of the principles, as well as those who have some suspension knowledge and want to consolidate their practice and hone their skills.


Part I: June 8th, 2026
Part II: June 15th, 2026
(ticket is for the ENTIRE SERIES)



This class does NOT require a TK/arms-in harness, all ties can also be done from a chest harness. Addie will offer options to suit a variety of needs, especially any that are expressed by class participants, so bring your questions and situations!

Between the two classes we will cover:


Discussion of safety, ways to get out of trouble quickly and elegantly.
Building a scene, interpersonal dynamics, and thoughts on communicating needs while maintaining those dynamics.
Information for those being tied, including nerve spotting, testing ties to find ‘hot spots’, and body mechanics tricks to help manage tension/strain.
Considerations when choosing suspension lines and some exercises to improve suspension line handling.
A progressable partial suspension with option to turn into full suspension – great practice for line management, body handling, and keeping focus on the ‘big picture’ and partner interactions.
Side suspension with options to add mini transitions – build this as complicated or straightforward as you want without making it harder to ‘exit’ smoothly.
‘Falling with style’ – a highly modifiable partial-to-full suspension progression focusing on lowering rather than lifting through a variety of positions. This is useful for those who want to stay closer to the ground, for tying folks who have concerns about grip strength, or in pairings where the person tying is smaller/lighter than the person being tied. This suspension can be done with a variety of upper body ties, including just a ‘safety’ line.
Time dependent, we will also learn a quick and easy suspensionable futomomo.

events.title: How To Play...
events.description:
Maybe you don’t know someone very well but both want to have fun, hot, or cute times with rope… how do you actually do that? Everyone wants to play, but many of us don’t know how.
This session looks at practical ways to start to actually play in rope (with new partner or maybe partners we know very well but feel a bit stuck with) beyond repeating the same patterns or keeping things so ‘safe’ and familiar that you never really drop into your flow where you can express what you want or discover something new.
For me… play needs a mix of curiosity and fantasy, a bit of vulnerability and confidence, mixed with a big dose of fuck around and find out… so what helps cultivate that? And how do we navigate the pleasure and risk of trying tying with someone new, doing this ‘play’, building trust as you go?
What will we cover


Negotiating and upholding care in these situations – what’s important to know?


How can you create a sense of narrative through roles, dynamics, and intentions?


How do you begin a session and work with its ‘flow’? (What does this even mean?)


What risks are you willing to take? What’s off limits? What consent practices actually work here?


How do you end things intentionally?


Let’s unpick a bit of this language and see what it looks like in practical senses. We’ll approach this through discussion, demo, and reflection, with space for your questions, ideas, and invitations to inspire your own exploration

events.title: Radical Inclusion
events.description:
The world can often feel divided and exclusionary. What would it mean to turn that on its head? This workshop explores how we can actively include ourselves and others, while acknowledging the real need for both inclusive and separatist spaces. 
Together, we will examine the barriers that create exclusion—such as access, power dynamics, and social norms—and explore practical ways to respond to them. The focus is on finding a balance between collective needs and individual experiences, and reimagining what truly supportive spaces can look like. 
Led by Caritia, this session offers a space for reflection, discussion, and collaborative thinking. Participants will be invited to design and imagine the kinds of groups and environments they would want to be part of, while developing tools to meaningfully include difference and diversity for the benefit of all. 
What we’ll cover


What “radical inclusion” means in practice 


The role of exclusion: boundaries, safety, and separatist spaces 


Identifying barriers to inclusion (access, identity, power) 


Balancing individual needs with group dynamics 


Designing spaces you would actually want to belong to 


Practical strategies for including difference and diversity

events.title: Meinberg/Greve/Wesley
events.description:
Lajos Meinberg grew up in a family of musicians, which nurtured his love for jazz from an early age. Since 2020, he has been studying at the Jazz Institute Berlin under Wolfgang Köhler, Tino Dorado, and Bastian Stein, and has been actively involved in the Berlin jazz scene since then. He has had the opportunity to perform with musicians such as Rodney Green, Doug Weiss, Matt Wilson and Martin Wind. Lajos received the Ingolf Burkhardt Award in 2022 and won first prize at the International Jazzhaus Piano Competition in Freiburg in 2024, as well as second prize at the International Jazz Piano Competition Lausanne in 2025. In August 2023, Lajos was part of the Elbphilharmonie Jazz Academy, where he had the chance to learn from musicians like Anat Cohen, Donny McCaslin, and Sullivan Fortner.
Johann Greve is a double bassist and composer from Lower Saxony. Since moving to Berlin in 2019, he has worked as a sideman on a wide variety of projects and established himself in the young Berlin jazz scene. He has performed with Percy Pursglove, Julius Gawlik, Charlotte Greve and Olga Reznichenko, among others. In March 2024, he recorded material for his debut album with his quartet.
California-born drummer Genius Wesley is an emerging force on the international jazz scene, known for his electrifying energy, deep musicality, and fearless improvisation. A prodigy percussionist, he has already performed with jazz greats such as David Binney, Sean Jones, Buster Williams, Azar Lawrence, Gerald Clayton, and many more.

The band Hunger, consisting of Christoph Rothmeier and Jörg Hochapfel, has been around since 1996, initially on Lake Constance, then for a long time in Hamburg, and finally in Berlin.
Previously known in the music world for their ""abstract pop studies with a Dadaist bent"" (taz) and ""nervous disco-punk racket"" (Tagesspiegel), they have in recent years moved into a somewhat quieter, but no less disorienting, musical territory between stumbling exotica and out-of-tune fake folk, using synthesizers, home organs, theremin, and homemade instruments.
They're bringing with them their brand-new album ""Trikotin,"" consisting of eight tracks improvised and subsequently refined in a secret French studio, available in the most practical and versatile format imaginable: a 36-page, lovingly risographed sheet music book!

This weekly class is designed for anyone who would like to learn about Japanese-inspired rope bondage/shibari/kinbaku whether you see yourself in the role of the person tying or being tied. We firmly believe that everyone, even if you wish to be tied, should know the absolute basics of this craft. 
What we do

We talk about what the heck is Japanese inspired rope bondage and why we call it “inspired”.
We show you the tools are we using and tell you why they are designed the way they are.
We talk about why people love to tie/get tied and what happens if you tie/get tied?
We show you the fundamental principles of shibari and first techniques you can immediately use
We talk about the history of shibari, give you pointers on anatomy, psychology and safety
We will tie ourselves, other people (if you and they want to) and actually take time to try stuff out and play, play, play

This class is suited for

all kinds of bodies (abled and non-abled), all gender expressions, all kinds of sexualities (including people on the ace-spectrum), all kind of brains (neurospicy or neurotypical, affected by trauma, etc.)
people coming solo or bringing a partner (or group), people who only want to tie their own bodies as well as people who want to tie/get tied by others

events.description:
This is our experimental shibari playground for all skill levels. Each month explores a new topic — from shame and semenawa to performance, advanced movement, or the mythical “3rd rope” in TKs. We rotate between two themes, always bringing new inspiration to your rope practice. Open to all levels with foundational knowledge. Bring your curiosity, your questions, and your rope. 
This month we are focusing on: pain – weather you call it s/m or semenawa, this class is all about exploring how to use rope to create pain. We will explore both external pain and uncomfortable body positions. This class is suitable for all skill levels. 
Play & Connection
These classes are dedicated to the research of the interpersonal, connective, and fun side of shibari. Forget about rope technique for a while and learn hands-on skills for actually playing with what you know. The topic varies from month to month, and can be anything from pain and predicament ties to fun games like rope fight club. Come learn the skills that take your sessions from good to fantastic!

events.description:
As a keyboardist, producer and improviser, Dan Nicholls embraces sound as a tool for liberation, healing and joyful collectivity. Intricately crafting sound worlds which invite listeners to explore both other-worldly perceptions and the grounding and embodying nature of sound and movement, Dan's work deeply considers how sonic (and other) gestures might facilitate forms of resistance, unity and deeper understanding. 

Dan has worked as a keyboardist with Alabaster De Plume, Goldie, Shabaka, Dudù Kouate, Dali De Saint Paul, Matthew Herbert, Sarah Nicolls, Christian Marklay, Squarepusher and many more.
They co-curate the London event series 'Free Movements' and have created music and sound design for dance, film and installations.
